explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. David says "For He has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the waters." So the LORD isn't just borrowing the earth. He laid its foundation Himself. That's a landlord who built the whole building, friend.

Close, but the psalm says otherwise. Right after "The earth is the LORD’s," David says "For He has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the waters." That little word "For" is David giving the reason. So the answer is True, and the LORD founded it Himself.

explanations.answer: Someone with clean hands and a pure heart
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David answers his own question: "He who has clean hands and a pure heart…" Nothing about resumes or fancy titles. I'll admit I checked my own hands after reading that one, and flour doesn't count.

explanations.answer: Someone from a famous family line
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since people love a big family name. But David never mentions family lines here. He says "He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to an idol or swear deceitfully." It's about the person's hands and heart, not whose name is on the mailbox.

explanations.answer: Someone who brings the biggest gift
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking. We all want to show up holding something impressive. But David names no gift at all. He says "He who has clean hands and a pure heart…" So this isn't about what's in your hands. It's about whether they're clean.

Not quite, friend. David says the one who may stand there "does not lift up his soul to an idol or swear deceitfully." So deceitful swearing is the opposite of what he describes. The answer is False, and it's right there in verse 4.

Yep, False. David describes the person who stands in the LORD's holy place as one who does not "swear deceitfully." He says it right alongside clean hands and a pure heart. No fine print on this one, baker.

That's it, baker. David says "He will receive blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation." Two gifts, and both come from God. Vindication means being set right, and that's a gift worth having.

I can see why you'd reach for it, but riches and long life never show up in this verse. David says "He will receive blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation." The text names blessing and vindication, so that's what I'm sticking with.

Nice thinking, since David was a king. But the psalm doesn't mention land or a kingdom here. It says "He will receive blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation." Those are the two things on the list.

Baked right, baker. David says "Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob." Seeking is the whole point. I think there's something warm in the word "face," like looking for someone you're glad to see.

Good try, since verse 1 is all about the earth. But David doesn't call them rulers. He calls them "the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob." The earth belongs to the LORD, so these folks are seekers.

The gates do show up soon after, so I get the mix-up. But the psalm doesn't describe this generation as gatekeepers. It says "Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob." They're seekers, not security.

You got it, baker. David says "Lift up your heads, O gates! Be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of Glory may enter!" The doors are told to open wide because the King is coming in. That's a door with a very good reason to move.
Easy to flip, but the direction is the other way. David says the doors are lifted "that the King of Glory may enter!" He's coming in, not heading out. Nobody's showing Him the exit in this psalm.

Resting sounds nice, I won't argue with that. But the psalm says "that the King of Glory may enter!" The doors lift so He can come through. The only rest in this psalm is that one word, Selah, at the end.
Perfect, baker. David answers, "The LORD strong and mighty…" The question was who the King of Glory is, and the answer is the LORD Himself. Strong and mighty, no hedging.
I see why that came to mind, since prophets speak for God. But the psalm's answer is "The LORD strong and mighty…" The King of Glory isn't a messenger. He's the LORD Himself.
A prince is a fair guess for a king story, friend. But David says "The LORD strong and mighty…" The King of Glory is no prince waiting for a turn. He's the LORD.

Not this time, baker. David says the King of Glory is "The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle." Nobody who is mighty in battle needs a bodyguard at the door. So the answer is False, and the doors lift for the strong one.
Right, it's False. The psalm calls Him "The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle." Strong and mighty is the opposite of weak. I think those doors had every reason to hurry up.

That's the one, baker. This time David answers, "The LORD of Hosts—He is the King of Glory." Same King, and this time the answer comes with a new name. Hosts means armies, and that title carries some weight.

That's a real title for God, so I see the pull. But it isn't the one in verse 10. The psalm says "The LORD of Hosts—He is the King of Glory." The God of Abraham is a good name, just not the one this answer uses.
That one's a real title for God too, so nice instinct. But it's not what Psalm 24 says. Verse 10 answers, "The LORD of Hosts—He is the King of Glory." That's the name the psalm lands on.
